summary:
Jammu and Kashmīr stands under India's national framework, where Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026. The amendment replaces the self-identification route inherited from the 2014 Supreme Court recognition and the 2019 Act with a scheme limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, to intersex individuals, and to male and female categories. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside legal recognition, and certification by a medical board and district authority becomes mandatory, including for gender-affirming surgery.

The amendment adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics counter that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. Coverage of the bill records it as approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent.

The most visitor-facing feature on file for Jammu and Kashmīr is structural and operational rather than legislative. Armed-forces jurisdiction under a special-powers act persists in parts of the territory, producing a heavy checkpoint-and-document regime at entry points and at internal checkpoints. That regime raises appearance-and-identity scrutiny for every traveller, and therefore specifically for anyone whose documents and presentation differ.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel in India. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment was passed amid protests in Mumbai, and the scale of the affected population is put at an estimated two million transgender people across India. The dispute over the bill is framed differently by each side: the government casts it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while the People's Union for Civil Liberties and rights activists cast the new offences as a return to colonial-era criminalisation.

India's position sits alongside a mixed regional picture on documentation and screening. The Allahabad High Court's February 2026 intervention on a passport medical examination shows courts willing to check administrative demands placed on trans applicants, while the CISF and Railway Protection Force incidents of 2024 show screening points acting on appearance rather than on documents presented.

The removal of gender-identity-specific offences in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is a national change with direct bearing on violence risk, and it is reported against a backdrop of trans communities expecting more assaults rather than fewer. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 offers a counterweight, recording limited and non-systemic police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jammu and Kashmīr who sought legal gender recognition through self-identification lose that route under the March 2026 amendment. Recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, to intersex people, and to male and female categories, with medical board and district authority certification required; self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people fall outside the scheme.

Gender-affirming surgery now requires medical-board and district-authority certification, which places a clinical gate in front of a procedure that the earlier framework treated as a matter of the person's own declaration. The 2019 Act's welfare framing survives in the government's justification, but the People's Union for Civil Liberties and other critics argue the new offences narrow rather than widen protection.

Residents retain the protections that flow from the Supreme Court's 2018 decriminalisation of same-sex acts and from constitutional non-discrimination on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable, though courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units for some purposes.

Sexual-violence protection weakened for residents in 2024 with the replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which dropped the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people. Police sensitisation and the ban on conversion therapy ordered in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police on 7 June 2021, together with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities, remain the principal protective guidance on record.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill is not confirmed in the sources on file; the coverage records it as approved by both houses and awaiting assent, so the operative text of the 2019 Act may still govern at the time of travel. Whether the amended recognition scheme has been notified for application in Jammu and Kashmīr specifically is unresolved and not sourced.

No incident of trans-specific violence, police abuse or document refusal occurring within Jammu and Kashmīr appears in the inventory. The checkpoint, custody, airport and passport cases cited here are documented in other Indian jurisdictions and are used as evidence of a national pattern, not as events in this territory.

The overlap between areas of armed-forces jurisdiction under the special-powers act and any documented treatment of trans travellers is not sourced. Nor is there data on enforcement rates under the new Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita offences, on the practical availability of medical certification for gender recognition, or on how the amendment interacts with existing identity documents held by residents.
